source_words: Scaled content abuse is when many pages are generated for the primary purpose of manipulating search rankings and not helping users. This abusive practice is typically focused on creating large amounts of unoriginal content that provides little to no value to users, no matter how it's created.
notes: Words match exactly. Footer 'Last updated 2026-08-28 UTC.' (before date_read; no change). 'However they are made' renders 'no matter how it's created'; the definition also turns on 'not helping users' and 'little to no value to users'.

source_words: Doorway abuse is when sites or pages are created to rank for specific, similar search queries. They lead users to intermediate pages that aren't as useful as the final destination.
notes: Exact. Last updated 2026-08-28 UTC.

source_words: Examples of doorway abuse include: ... Having multiple domain names or pages targeted at specific regions or cities that funnel users to one page; Generating pages to funnel visitors into the actual usable or relevant portion of a site
notes: Exact; one of four listed examples of doorway abuse. 'Elsewhere' is the claim's gloss; Google says 'into the actual usable or relevant portion of a site'.

source_words: Creating substantially similar pages that are closer to search results than a clearly defined, browseable hierarchy
notes: Exact, and listed as an example of doorway abuse (stronger than 'a sign'). Google's contrast is pages that resemble search results versus a clearly defined, browseable hierarchy; 'a hierarchy is the remedy' is the worker's inference (labelled as such), not Google's words; 'near-duplicate' paraphrases 'substantially similar'.

source_words: Answering yes to some or all of the questions below is a warning sign that you should reevaluate how you're creating content: ... Are you writing to a particular word count because you've heard or read that Google has a preferred word count? (No, we don't.)
notes: Exact. Footer 'Last updated 2026-10-05 UTC.' (before date_read; no change).

source_words: Answering yes to some or all of the questions below is a warning sign that you should reevaluate how you're creating content: ... Are you using extensive automation to produce content on many topics?
notes: Exact; 'warning sign' is Google's own lead-in to the search-engine-first list. Last updated 2026-10-05 UTC.

source_words: Does the content present information in a way that makes you want to trust it, such as clear sourcing, evidence of the expertise involved, background about the author or the site that publishes it, such as through links to an author page or a site's About page?
notes: Exact (the CSV stops before 'such as through links to an author page or a site's About page?'). A self-assessment question, not a statement about ranking. Last updated 2026-10-05 UTC.

source_words: This new policy builds on our previous spam policy about automatically-generated content, ensuring that we can take action on scaled content abuse as needed, no matter whether content is produced through automation, human efforts, or some combination of human and automated processes.
notes: Post 'What web creators should know about our March 2024 core update and new spam policies', dated 'Tuesday, March 5, 2024'. Sentence exact.

source_words: Flat hierarchies tend to work well if you have distinct, recognizable categories, because people don't have to click through as many levels. ... All other things being equal, deep hierarchies are more difficult to use.
notes: Kathryn Whitenton, NN/g, November 10, 2013 (dateModified 2024-08-02). The article also says 'there's no single right answer, and going too far to either extreme will backfire', and 'Categories that are specific and do not overlap are the easiest to understand.'

source_words: Abstract: '... increased depth did harm search performance on the web, a medium condition of depth and breadth outperformed the broadest shallow web structure overall.' Body: 'there was no significant difference between the 16x32 and the 32x16 hierarchies for reaction time.'
correction: The words are the abstract's own, but the paper's results don't show the medium structure beating the broadest one. With 19 subjects and three structures (8x8x8; 16x32; 32x16), the three-level 8x8x8 was significantly slower than both two-level structures (ANOVA F(2,36)=6.34, Bonferroni post-hoc). 16x32 (mean 36 s) against 32x16 (46 s) was not significant, 8x8x8 averaging 58 s, and 32x16 was ranked most preferred more often (Table 2). Read: depth hurt; medium against broadest is an untested lead in speed, and preference went to the broadest.
notes: Read the paper itself (the PDF linked from the Microsoft Research page; text via pdftotext, scan-quality) and the page's abstract. Larson & Czerwinski, CHI 98, April 1998.

source_words: The comparisons showed that static was significantly faster than adaptive for all three orders. ... Although the adaptable menu was preferred by the majority of subjects (55%), the adaptive menu did have support (30%). By contrast, only 15% of subjects wanted the static menu
notes: Read the paper itself (Findlater & McGrenere, 'A Comparison of Static, Adaptive, and Adaptable Menus', CHI 2004); 'a controlled lab study with 27 subjects'. Left out of the claim: the static menu was the optimal split menu, built from item frequencies 'known in advance of the task, as was done in our experiment', and 15% wanted it 'even though it was the optimal split menu'. Adaptable was not significantly different from static unless it came first, when it was significantly slower.

source_words: The main grouping guidelines are: ... Keep a medium level of granularity. Don't offer huge groups with numerous options that require extensive time to scan. ... Use concise, yet descriptive labels for each group. || [characteristics] Everything visible at once — no scrolling
correction: Two of the three are grouping guidelines, and the labels are 'concise, yet descriptive', not 'distinct'. 'Everything visible at once — no scrolling' is not a guideline: it is in the article's list of the characteristics that define a mega menu ('mega menus have the following characteristics: ...').
notes: Jakob Nielsen and Angie Li, NN/g, March 26, 2017 (dateModified 2023-06-27). The granularity guideline goes both ways: 'don't make the individual groups so small that the mega menu has an overabundance of groups'. 'Distinct' appears only in the screenshot captions.
